readings.title: Rip Van Winkle: the motto and Knickerbocker’s introduction
readings.challenge: Read the introduction as a joke told with a straight face. Mark each sentence that seems to praise Knickerbocker and then quietly takes the praise back.
readings.focus: Irving frames his tale with a solemn oath to truth and a mock-respectful portrait of the invented historian who supposedly found it.
readings.context: Washington Irving (1783–1859) published “Rip Van Winkle” in The Sketch Book (1819–20), presenting it as a tale found among the papers of Diedrich Knickerbocker, an invented old historian of Dutch New York; this text follows a 1919 London edition. Irving had already published, in 1809, a comic History of New York under Knickerbocker’s name, which made fun of the colony’s Dutch founders and offended some of their descendants; “Knickerbocker” soon became a nickname for New Yorkers. The motto is from a play by William Cartwright, a seventeenth-century English writer; Woden is the old Germanic god whose name survives in “Wednesday.” Burghers are citizens of a town; black-letter is the heavy old style of type used in early printed books; “more in sorrow than in anger” is a phrase from Shakespeare’s Hamlet. A Waterloo medal, given to soldiers of the 1815 battle, and a Queen Anne’s farthing, an old coin, each carried a royal portrait.

excerpt.locator: Rip Van Winkle (1919), the verse motto and the introduction before the tale; opens “By Woden, God of Saxons, From whence comes Wensday, that is Wodensday. Truth is a thing…”; closes “…almost equal to the being stamped on a Waterloo medal, or a Queen Anne’s farthing.”.

questions.prompt: The motto swears by a pagan god to keep the truth until the grave. Why might Irving open a tale about a man who sleeps twenty years with an oath of truthfulness?
facilitatorNotes: It is a comic warning: the more a storyteller swears to the truth, the more we suspect a tall tale. The odd oath “By Woden” makes the solemnity sound old-fashioned and a little absurd.
The motto also prepares for the German and Dutch background of the story. Readers who have finished the tale can connect it to the Note, which insists the story is “beyond the possibility of doubt.”
evidence: Truth is a thing that ever I will keep

questions.prompt: What kind of historian is Knickerbocker? Explain the comparison of a Dutch farmhouse to “a little clasped volume of black-letter.”
facilitatorNotes: He studies people rather than books, because books on his subject are scarce; old burghers and especially their wives are full of “legendary lore.” He reads a family the way a scholar reads a rare old book, with “the zeal of a book-worm.”
Irving praises oral tradition as “invaluable to true history” while hinting that legends and history are not the same. Ask whether his method is good history, good storytelling, or both.
evidence: His historical researches, however, did not lie so much among books as among men
he looked upon it as a little clasped volume of black-letter, and studied it with the zeal of a book-worm

questions.prompt: Find the sentences where praise turns into its opposite. What is the joke in “it is not a whit better than it should be” and in the claims about the history’s “scrupulous accuracy”?
facilitatorNotes: “Not a whit better than it should be” sounds like praise but means it is no better than it ought to be, with a hint of a bad reputation. Its accuracy was “a little questioned” at first, and its acceptance “into all historical collections” is a joke on a book that was in fact a comic invention.
Irving is teasing his own earlier book and its critics. Students can find other double-edged phrases, such as the remark that Knickerbocker’s time “might have been much better employed.”
evidence: to tell the truth, it is not a whit better than it should be
Its chief merit is its scrupulous accuracy, which indeed was a little questioned on its first appearance

questions.prompt: How is Knickerbocker remembered, according to the last paragraph? What makes the comparison with a Waterloo medal or a Queen Anne’s farthing funny?
facilitatorNotes: His hobby did “now and then kick up the dust a little” and grieved some friends, yet he is remembered “more in sorrow than anger,” and biscuit-bakers have put his face on New Year cakes. Being printed on a cake is set beside being stamped on a war medal or royal coin, a mock-heroic form of fame that gets eaten.
The passage gently answers the people Irving’s History had offended. Ask what kind of “immortality” a storyteller can hope for.
evidence: his errors and follies are remembered “more in sorrow than anger,”
particularly by certain biscuit-bakers, who have gone so far as to imprint his likeness on their new-year cakes

readings.title: Rip Van Winkle: the Note and the Postscript
readings.challenge: Read the Note as a piece of evidence and judge it as a lawyer would. Then read the Postscript for its images of weather and for a story that echoes Rip’s.
readings.focus: A mock proof that a tall tale is true, and older mountain legends that surround it.
readings.context: Washington Irving (1783–1859) published “Rip Van Winkle” in The Sketch Book (1819–20), presenting it as a tale found among the papers of Diedrich Knickerbocker, an invented old historian of Dutch New York; this text follows a 1919 London edition. In the tale, the easygoing Rip wanders into the Catskill Mountains, drinks from the flagon of a strange crew of old Dutchmen playing ninepins, sleeps twenty years, and returns to find the American Revolution over. Frederick “der Rothbart” (Barbarossa, “Red-beard”) is a German emperor said in legend to sleep inside the Kyffhäuser mountain. A document “signed with a cross” was signed by someone who could not write. Manitou is a word from Algonquian languages for a spirit or spiritual power; “propitiated” means calmed with offerings; carded cotton has been combed into fluffy strands; “beetling” means overhanging; a bittern is a marsh bird. The Kaaterskill is a real creek in the Catskills.
readings.contentNote: The Postscript uses the period terms “Indians” and “red men” and the offensive word “squaw,” and retells Native beliefs secondhand, as a white writer’s picturesque legend.

excerpt.locator: Rip Van Winkle (1919), the Note and Postscript that follow the tale; opens “The foregoing tale, one would suspect, had been suggested to Mr. Knickerbocker by a…”; closes “…to the present day, being the identical stream known by the name of the Kaaters-kill.”.

questions.prompt: Knickerbocker’s note claims the story is “beyond the possibility of doubt.” Examine his evidence. Why is it funny?
facilitatorNotes: He says the Dutch settlements are naturally full of marvels, that he has heard stranger stories, and that Rip was “rational and consistent on every other point.” His final proof is a certificate “signed with a cross, in the justice’s own handwriting”: the witness could not write, and the justice wrote it himself, so it proves nothing.
The narrator has just admitted the tale may come from a German legend, then hands over to Knickerbocker’s solemn defence. Irving is mocking pompous historians and enjoying his own fiction.
evidence: shows that it is an absolute fact, narrated with his usual fidelity
signed with a cross, in the justice’s own handwriting
The story, therefore, is beyond the possibility of doubt.

questions.prompt: How does the Postscript picture the spirit who rules the weather? Choose an image and explain its effect.
facilitatorNotes: She hangs up new moons and cuts old ones into stars; she spins summer clouds “out of cobwebs and morning dew” like carded cotton. Household crafts (cutting, spinning, carding) make vast forces homely and gentle.
When angry, she sits in black clouds “like a bottle-bellied spider in the midst of its web.” The same spinning becomes menacing; the image turns a storm over the valleys into a trap.
evidence: She hung up the new moons in the skies, and cut up the old ones into stars.
she would spin light summer clouds out of cobwebs and morning dew
like a bottle-bellied spider in the midst of its web

questions.prompt: How does the story of the hunter at the Garden Rock echo Rip’s? What does the Postscript add to the tale?
facilitatorNotes: Both men stray into a haunted part of the mountains and take something belonging to the spirits: Rip drinks from their flagon, the hunter seizes a gourd. Rip’s punishment is gentle and comic; the hunter is swept to his death, and the stream still flows “to the present day.”

The Postscript surrounds Rip’s tale with older legends of the same mountains. But they come secondhand, as “Indian traditions” from Knickerbocker’s notebook; students may ask whose stories these are, and how far Irving’s retelling can be trusted.
evidence: a hunter who had lost his way penetrated to the Garden Rock
One of these he seized and made off with it
the identical stream known by the name of the Kaaters-kill
